value.overview: Heermann's Gull (Larus heermanni) is a medium-sized Pacific gull that breeds mainly on islands in Mexico's Gulf of California. It is distinctive for its medium-gray body, dark wings, black legs, and red bill in adults. After breeding, many birds move north along the Pacific coast, while others disperse southward. The species is strongly associated with marine environments and is rarely found far inland. Most of the world's population depends on a small number of breeding colonies.
value.classification: Heermann's Gull belongs to the gull family Laridae and the shorebird order Charadriiformes. Its scientific name is Larus heermanni.
value.identification: Adults have a medium-gray body, dark gray to blackish wings, a dark tail with white edging, black legs, and a red bill with a black tip. The head is mostly white in breeding plumage but becomes dusky or mottled outside the breeding season. Juveniles are darker brown-gray overall, with a dark bill that gradually develops paler and reddish areas as they mature. Its combination of gray body, dark wings, and black legs is distinctive among Pacific coast gulls.
value.rangeHabitat: Heermann's Gull breeds mainly on rocky, sparsely vegetated islands in the Gulf of California and along the Pacific coast of western Mexico, with smaller colonies farther north. Outside the breeding season it uses beaches, rocky shores, estuaries, coastal lagoons, bays, offshore waters, and other marine habitats from western Mexico north to the Pacific coast of the United States and, less regularly, British Columbia and southward. In Costa Rica it is an exceptionally rare Pacific-coast visitor or accidental species, with a possible record from Chomes, Puntarenas, on December 6, 1985; it is not a regular or established coastal gull there.
value.migrationStatus: A seasonal migrant and post-breeding disperser. Many birds move northward after nesting, reaching the western United States and occasionally British Columbia, while some disperse south along the Pacific coast. In Costa Rica, occurrence is extremely rare and appears to involve occasional southward dispersal or vagrancy, mainly during the northern winter rather than regular migration.
value.breeding: Breeding is highly colonial and takes place mainly from spring into early summer on small islands in the Gulf of California. Isla Rasa supports the great majority of the global breeding population. Nests are simple scrapes placed on bare soil, rock, or guano-covered ground, often in dense colonies. A typical clutch contains two or three eggs. Both adults defend the nest and feed the young, which remain dependent on marine food brought back from nearby waters.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small marine fish, especially schooling species such as sardines and anchovies, along with squid, crustaceans, mollusks, and other marine invertebrates. Heermann's Gulls also scavenge carrion, refuse, and fishing waste. They frequently follow Brown Pelicans and attempt to seize fish disturbed or dropped by the larger birds. Feeding occurs in coastal waters, around beaches and estuaries, and near fishing activity.
value.behavior: Heermann's Gulls are social and highly gregarious, especially at breeding colonies and communal roosts. They fly strongly over coastal waters, swim readily, and gather in mixed flocks with other gulls and terns outside the breeding season. Adults can be aggressive when defending nests and may mob predators or competing birds. Many individuals show strong attachment to breeding or nonbreeding sites, while post-breeding movements can cover large distances along the Pacific coast.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population increased substantially after protection reduced historical egg harvesting, but the overall current trend is uncertain. Numbers can fluctuate sharply with marine conditions, food availability, and events such as El Niño, and recent regional monitoring has indicated declines in some nonbreeding areas.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include the concentration of most breeding birds in a few colonies, disturbance at nesting sites, reduced availability of small pelagic fish, accidental capture or conflict with fisheries, pollution, and predation or competition involving introduced or human-associated mammals and other gulls. Climate-driven changes in ocean productivity may further affect breeding success and food supplies.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and carefully manage seabird breeding islands, coastal wetlands, estuaries, and nearshore waters. Avoid disturbing nesting colonies and roosting flocks, keep dogs and other animals away from sensitive coastal sites, reduce plastic and other marine pollution, and support sustainable fisheries. In Costa Rica, report any suspected sighting with photographs and precise location details because records are exceptionally rare and valuable for documenting the species' occasional occurrence.
